issues.issue: This names DSI Lending Resources as "the lender," while paragraph 1 of the Arbitration Provision separately defines "the Lender" as "any Lender who provides you with a loan as a result of our services." Which definition controls the many later references to "Lender" is not resolved.

The obligation is only to "attempt to" obtain a loan, issue an LOC and assist with documents, with no standard of effort stated. What performance discharges the promise for which the CAB fee is charged is left open.

A one-day estimated performance period sits awkwardly with the additional services in the following sentence that "may be provided throughout the term," leaving the period over which the CAB fee is earned unclear.

Services (4)-(8) are qualified by open-ended conditions — "if requested," "where available," "certain CAB services" — with no benchmark for performance. Whether any of them was ever owed or performed cannot be measured from the text.
"The term" is undefined — it could mean the term of the arranged loan, of the LOC, or of this Agreement — and "may be provided" makes the obligation permissive rather than binding.

The finance charge is described as depending on amount and term, yet the Cost and Payment Terms fix it at a stated $561.15 for this transaction. The two statements can be harmonised but sit in tension.
The 708.90% CAB-fee rate is stated against the APR of 713.38% disclosed later in the same section, and the relationship between the two figures is not explained.
The number of payments is written "LO payments," which is not a number; the count of instalments has to be reconstructed from the payment schedule.
The stated $3.00 of lender interest cannot be reconciled with the 10% per annum rate on a $300 loan running from April to August recited in the Description of Our Services and in the APR sentence.

"[T]he Total of Payments is $86.15" is a mechanical error: ten payments of $86.15 with a final payment of $85.80 total $861.15, not $86.15. The figure as written states the wrong aggregate obligation.
"[P]rorated daily basis for the final period" does not identify what "the final period" is or how the refund is computed, so the amount refundable on prepayment cannot be derived from the text.
"[Y]our finance charge may be reduced" is permissive and indefinite, while the preceding sentence states an entitlement to a prorated CAB-fee refund.
"[A]ttorneys' fees, and costs of collection" is an unqualified catch-all appended to specific dollar-fixed items, with no reasonableness limit here (unlike the Collection Expenses paragraph).
A late charge "equal to the greater of 5% or $7.50" does not say 5% of what — the instalment, the unpaid balance, or the loan — leaving the charge indeterminate.

The sentence is scrambled — the heading and clauses are interleaved ("You rec ... licable, on Chapter $ of the Texas Business and Commerce Code") — so the LOC request and its cap are not readable as written.

Default limb (2), "if you fail to perform your other promises [to] us," has no materiality or cure qualifier and reaches every undertaking in the document, including the warranties in the signature block.

Limb (3) makes failure of obligations owed to the Lender a default under this Agreement, although the Description of Our Services states "We are not a lender" and the loan is a separate contract with DSI.
"[L]ess any unearned charges" is not defined and does not say how the unearned portion of the CAB fee is computed on acceleration.

The right to "seek collection of any check or similar security you have provided us" runs up against the Collection Expenses paragraph's bar on threatening or pursuing criminal charges over a check given as security, and the boundary between them is exactly what a dispute would turn on.
"[A]ny other right or remedy allowed by law and this Agreement" is an open catch-all following one enumerated remedy, leaving its reach (and whether it embraces non-civil measures) uncertain.

This anti-waiver term ("we may waive or delay enforcing our rights without losing them") bears directly on whether conduct inconsistent with the Waiver of Jury Trial and Arbitration Provision forfeits the right to compel arbitration, and the two must be read together.

"[W]e are not required to file suit or arbitrate" sits against paragraph 4 of the Arbitration Provision, under which any dispute "shall be resolved by binding arbitration" upon election, raising a question about the seller's freedom to pursue other avenues of collection.

A jury-trial waiver "in the event of litigation arising out of or related to this Agreement" presupposes litigation, while the Arbitration Provision and paragraph 2(b) purport to remove disputes from court altogether.

It refers to a "Jury Trial Waiver and Arbitration Agreement" that you may "reject," whereas the document itself contains a "Waiver of Jury Trial and Arbitration Provision" with an opt-out process; whether these are the same instrument, and what happens to the jury waiver if the customer opts out, is not stated.

A "reasonable opportunity of not less than 60 days to cure the claim" gives an open-ended period whose outer bound is unstated, and "any claim that this agreement or related matter ... is legally non-compliant" is of uncertain reach.
This condition precedent to "initiating any claim" is hard to square with paragraph 4's right to demand arbitration "at any time" and paragraph 6's retained right to go to a small claims tribunal.

"Any corrective action shall relieve us and Lender of any liability" does not say what corrective action suffices or whether it must fully redress the claim, so the discharge it confers has no measurable boundary.
"[R]easonable" qualifies only the attorneys' fees, while "all costs and disbursements" is unqualified and unbounded, and fees are payable even if no proceedings are filed.

The bar on threatening or pursuing criminal charges over a check given as security is qualified by "in the absence of forgery, fraud, theft, or other criminal conduct" — a general catch-all against enumerated specifics whose reach (and who decides that such conduct exists) is exactly what the parties would fight over.

Phrased impersonally as "A person may not," it does not say that it binds the seller, and it pulls against the Default section's rights to "seek collection of any check or similar security" and to "exercise any other right or remedy allowed by law."

The description that arbitrating parties "waive their rights to file a lawsuit and proceed in court" overstates the operative bargain, which preserves small claims adjudication under paragraph 6 and court determination of the class waiver under paragraph 3.
"[A]n opportunity to present some evidence" is indefinite — "some" sets no floor on the evidentiary opportunity a party is guaranteed.

"[T]he broadest possible meaning" plus an open "without limitation" list leaves the outer scope of arbitrable "disputes" — including claims against unnamed "related third parties" and any "Lender" — to be argued over.

Sub-paragraph (a) commits "the validity and scope of this Arbitration Provision" to arbitration, but paragraph 3 provides that the validity and enforceability of the class waiver is "determined solely by a court ... and not by the arbitrator."

The class and representative waiver is the very provision whose invalidity, under paragraph 8, voids the whole Arbitration Provision, while paragraph 3 also supplies a different fallback; the interaction of those consequences is unsettled.

"[A]ll disputes ... shall be resolved by binding arbitration only on an individual basis" is expressly subject to paragraph 6, which retains small claims adjudication, so which disputes must actually be arbitrated depends on reconciling the two.

Reserving the validity of the class waiver "solely" to a court contradicts paragraph 1(a), which sends "the validity and scope of this Arbitration Provision and any claim or attempt to set aside" it to the arbitrator.

The fallback is triggered only if the arbitrator "fails or refuses to abide by" the waiver AND the court refuses to enforce it — a conjunctive condition that cannot occur in the order stated once paragraph 3 gives the court sole say.

This court-fallback provision overlaps with paragraph 8, under which invalidity of the class waiver renders the entire Arbitration Provision void, and the two prescribe different machinery for the same contingency.

The right to demand arbitration "at any time, even if the other party has begun a lawsuit" must be read with the Notices and Waivers clause preserving delayed enforcement, and it is the provision a party resisting waiver of arbitration would invoke.
The customer's "choice" of any other arbitrator is limited to one "reasonably satisfactory to us," a standard the seller applies with no stated criteria.

Naming the AAA and JAMS as selectable organisations cannot easily be squared with the later sentence in the same paragraph barring selection of "any arbitration organization that permits class actions in arbitration."

Excluding any organisation "that permits class actions in arbitration" cannot be reconciled with the immediately preceding sentence offering the customer the AAA and JAMS, whose published rules do provide for class or representative proceedings.

The $1,000 cap on advanced filing, administrative and hearing fees conflicts with paragraph 5, which promises that "at your request we will advance your portion of the arbitration expenses" without any cap.
"[A]ny circumstances that the party contends might preclude arbitration" is open-ended and self-defined by the contending party, so what triggers the 30-day notice duty cannot be fixed.

This 30-day notice-and-remedy requirement sits against the earlier sentence in the same paragraph permitting a demand for arbitration "at any time," and against the separate 60-day pre-suit notice provision.
The unqualified promise to advance "your portion of the arbitration expenses" on request conflicts with paragraph 4, which limits any such advance to "up to $1000."

The sentence first makes each party bear its own attorneys' fees and expenses and then preserves "any party's ability to recover costs and attorneys' fees to the extent authorized by law," leaving the fee rule self-cancelling.
The venue guarantee of the customer's county is undone by "or in such other place as shall be ordered by the arbitrator," which is subject to no stated limit.

Forbidding the arbitrator to apply any rules of civil procedure sits awkwardly with the preceding sentence authorising motions "substantially similar to a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim or a motion for summary judgment," which are creatures of those rules.
"[A] decision or an award in your favor resolving the dispute" does not say whether partial or mixed relief counts, so the fee consequence turns on an undefined outcome.

Mandatory reimbursement by an unsuccessful customer is hard to square with paragraph 4, which leaves it to "the arbitrator [to] decide whether we, Lender, or you ... will ultimately be responsible to pay those fees."

The retained small claims right must be reconciled with paragraph 4, under which "any dispute shall be resolved by binding arbitration" upon election by either side, and with paragraph 2(b)'s waiver of any court other than a small claims tribunal.

"[C]annot be adjudicated within the jurisdiction of a small claims tribunal" does not say whether the test is the amount claimed, the relief sought or the type of claim, leaving the boundary of the carve-out uncertain.

Routing any appeal from a small claims judgment into binding arbitration is in tension with the preceding sentence retaining the small claims forum, since in Texas such an appeal is a trial de novo in the county court.
The Arbitration Provision is made to benefit "related third parties," a class defined only by an inclusive list in paragraph 1(g), so which non-signatories may enforce it is open.

This poison-pill severability rule — invalidity of the class-arbitration waiver voids the entire Arbitration Provision — cannot be squared with the Entire Agreement clause, under which an invalid provision "shall be reformed if practicable" and "shall not in any way affect the remaining provisions."

The opt-out sentence is garbled and the address is given twice in corrupted form ("PL. Juan Store of Texas, Inc., Attn: Arbitration Opt-Ou"), so the place to which notice must be sent is not cleanly stated.

The carve-out making the Arbitration Provision governed by the FAA must be read with paragraph 7, which substitutes Texas arbitration law if a court finds the FAA inapplicable, and with the Texas-law rule for the rest of the Agreement.

The integration clause claims this is the entire agreement "relating to the subject matter," yet the document itself contemplates a separate "Jury Trial Waiver and Arbitration Agreement," a separate lender loan contract and the attached cancellation notices.

This reformation-and-survival rule contradicts paragraph 8 of the Arbitration Provision, under which invalidity of the class-arbitration waiver renders "this entire Arbitration Provision ... void" rather than being reformed or severed.
The list of documents acknowledged as received is broken and incomplete — "(1) A SEPARATE If T; 2) THIS ZES AGREEMENT" — so what the customer is certifying receipt of cannot be read off the clause.

The certification that the customer agrees to "the binding Waiver Of Jury Trial And Arbitration Provision" is difficult to square with the Opt-Out Process, which allows rejection of that provision within 90 days of the same signing.

The warranty of no intention to file for bankruptcy sits against paragraph 8 of the Arbitration Provision, which expressly contemplates that the customer's obligations may be "discharged through bankruptcy."
"[L]egitimate, open, and active" is undefined and the warranty fixes no point in time at which the account must have that character, though the whole consequence of a returned item turns on it.

This account warranty interacts directly with the Collection Expenses paragraph barring criminal charges over a check given as security "in the absence of forgery, fraud, theft, or other criminal conduct," since breach of the warranty is what would be said to supply that conduct.
"[F]or the duration of the services or any subsequent services" gives the information-sharing consent no fixed end point and "any information" no subject-matter limit.

The cancellation period runs from "the date of the transaction," while the attached Notice of Cancellation measures three days from "the date the contract is signed," and the two dates need not coincide.
The three-day period runs from "the date the contract is signed," whereas the NOTICE in the body of the Agreement runs it from "the date of the transaction."
The promise to return "any payment made by you under this contract" is awkward against the Cost and Payment Terms, under which the CAB fee is not paid up front but financed into the lender's loan.
